Monochromatic kk in a row

Kuo-Han Ku
Mathematics Division, National Center for Theoretical Sciences, National Taiwan University, Taipei 10617, Taiwan. Email: kuohan_ku@ncts.ntu.edu.tw.
Abstract

We study a variant of the kk-in-a-row game in which players alternatively claim positions until a kk-in-a-row is created among all claimed positions. This leads to the constraint near kk-in-a-row avoiding on configurations and the associated problem of determining their extremal densities of such configurations on a given board BB.

We investigate this problem on two types of boards: the grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and hypercubes [k]d[k]^{d}. For the grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we establish nearly tight bounds on the maximum density D⁡(k,ℤ2)D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}), showing that D⁡(k,ℤ2)=1−2kD(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=1-\frac{2}{k} whenever 3∤k3\nmid k, and determine both D⁡(3,ℤ2)D(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) and d⁡(3,ℤ2)d(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) exactly. We also bound the minimum density d⁡(k,ℤ2)d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) up to a gap of (8+o⁡(1))​k−1(8+o(1))k^{-1}. For hypercubes [k]d[k]^{d}, we derive asymptotic bounds on D⁡(k,[k]d)D(k,[k]^{d}) up to order k−2k^{-2} and obtain the exact value of d⁡(k,[k]d)d(k,[k]^{d}). Our results contrast with the classical no-(k+1)(k+1)-in-line problem, a similar problem imposing different constraint, where the trivial upper bound is conjectured to be attainable.

1 Introduction

Five-in-a-row, also known as “Gomoku”, is a strategy board game played on a 15×1515\times 15 grid. Two players take turns placing stones of their respective color on the board. The winner is the first to form a consecutive line of five or more stones of their color. Variants of five-in-a-row have been extensively studied, particularly in positional game theory. Using computer-assisted analysis, Allis [1] showed that standard and free Gomoku are first-player wins. On the other hand, the 99-in-a-row game played on the infinite grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} is a draw; a drawing strategy for the second player is given in [3].

Now imagine playing Five-in-a-row, but with two rules changed. First, all players place stones of the same color. Second, a player wins by occupying the last empty position of a five-in-a-row. We call this variant Monochromatic Five-in-a-row.

Under these new rules, the nature of the game changes completely. Rather than attacking and blocking the opponent, players must avoid creating a five-in-a-row with exactly one empty position, which we call a near five-in-a-row. Such a pattern appears only in the last two moves. If one player creates a near five-in-a-row, the other player completes it and wins.

This leads to the fundamental question: how long can such a game last? Clearly, the length of the game is capped by maxS∈𝒮⁡|S|+2\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}}|S|+2, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the family of subsets forbidding near five-in-a-rows. More generally, we can consider the monochromatic kk-in-a-row played on a given board BB, where k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, and define the family of saturated configurations 𝒮k​(B):=max⁡({S⊆B:|L\S|≥2​∀ k-in-a-row L})\mathcal{S}_{k}(B):=\max(\{S\subseteq B:|L\backslash S|\geq 2\ \forall\text{ $k$-in-a-row $L$}\})11 1 max⁡(𝒫)\max(\mathcal{P}) denotes the set of maximal elements in a poset 𝒫\mathcal{P}. for this game. Then the following question comes up.

Question.

Given a board BB and an integer k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, how does the spectrum of densities of the near kk-in-a-row avoiding family 𝒮k​(B)\mathcal{S}_{k}(B) behave? In particular, what can we say about the extrema of the spectrum?

A closely related problem in Combinatorial Geometry is the “No-(k+1)(k+1)-in-line” problem, which asks for the maximum size of a subset of a grid (typically [n]2[n]^{2} or ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}) containing no (k+1)(k+1) collinear points. The trivial upper bound for such subsets is k​nkn, and it is conjectured that this bound can be attained for all n≥kn\geq k. In contrast, our results show that, for the problem considered here, the trivial upper bound, 1−2k1-\frac{2}{k}, cannot be achieved in certain setting.

Remarkably, Grebennikov and Kwan [6] recently proved that the bound k​nkn is indeed achievable whenever n≥k≥1037n\geq k\geq 10^{37}. For small values of kk, the conjecture has been verified in several cases [2, 4, 5], while it remains open in general. In the case k=2k=2, the problem reduces to the classical no-three-in-line problem. The best known lower bound, (1.5+o⁡(1))​n(1.5+o(1))n, comes from a construction of Hall, Jackson, Sudbery, and Wild [7].

In this paper, two types of boards, the grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and hypercubes [k]d[k]^{d}, are concerned. Our main results give bounds on the extrema, D⁡(k,B)D(k,B) and d⁡(k,B)d(k,B), of density spectrum for these boards. The two cases require different techniques.

First, we look at the infinite grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}. As we cannot directly define such density on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, in order to approach ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we start from a finite grid board B=[ℓ]2B=[\ell]^{2} and take ℓ\ell to infinity. Denote D⁡(k,ℤ2):=limℓ→∞D⁡(k,[ℓ]2)D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}):=\lim\limits_{\ell\to\infty}D(k,[\ell]^{2}) and d⁡(k,ℤ2):=limℓ→∞d⁡(k,[ℓ]2)d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}):=\lim\limits_{\ell\to\infty}d(k,[\ell]^{2}). Later, the existence and uniqueness of these limits will be proved. For k=3k=3, both limits are determined.

Theorem 1.1.

D⁡(3,ℤ2)=15D(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=\frac{1}{5} and d⁡(3,ℤ2)=117.d(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=\frac{1}{17}.

For general kk, we obtain the following nearly tight bound on the upper limit,

Theorem 1.2.

For k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}, we have D⁡(k,ℤ2)∈[1−2k−1,1−2k]D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\in\left[1-\frac{2}{k-1},1-\frac{2}{k}\right]. Further, if kk is not a multiple of 33, it achieves upper bound, i.e., D⁡(k,ℤ2)=1−2kD(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=1-\frac{2}{k}.

and bounds on the lower limit with a gap (8+o⁡(1))​k−1(8+o(1))k^{-1}.

Theorem 1.3.

We have the bounds on the lower limit

d⁡(k,ℤ2)∈[1−16​k−1−o⁡(k−1),1−8​k−1+o⁡(k−1)]\displaystyle d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\in[1-16k^{-1}-o(k^{-1}),1-8k^{-1}+o(k^{-1})]

as kk grows.

For the second type, the minimum density is known. For the maximum density, we study the extremal behaviour as kk goes to infinity while dd fixed, and derive asymptotic bounds on the maximum density to the second order of k−1k^{-1}.

Theorem 1.4.

For d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, we have D⁡(k,[k]d)=1−2​k−1−O⁡(k−2)D(k,[k]^{d})=1-2k^{-1}-O(k^{-2}) as kk grows.

Theorem 1.5.

For k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} and d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, we have d⁡(k,[k]d)=(1−2k)dd(k,[k]^{d})=\left(1-\frac{2}{k}\right)^{d}.

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the necessary definitions and propositions. We discuss the grid in Section 3, and hypercubes in Section 4. Section 5 contains conjectures, variants, and possible directions for future research.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the basic notions used throughout the paper, including kk-boards, kk-lines, and near kk-lines, and describe several common examples. We then define saturated configurations and extremal densities formally. Finally, we prove two important propositions concerning the infinite grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}.

Definition 2.1.

Let k∈ℕ≥3k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}. Given a set BB and a kk-uniform subset family ℒ⊆(Bk)\mathcal{L}\subseteq\binom{B}{k}. The pair (B,ℒ)(B,\mathcal{L}) is called a kk-board. A subset S∈ℒS\in\mathcal{L} is called a kk-line. A subset S′⊆BS^{\prime}\subseteq B is called a near kk-line if |S′|=k−1|S^{\prime}|=k-1 and S′⊆SS^{\prime}\subseteq S for some kk-line SS.

In the following we focus on grid-shaped boards that arise from extensions of the classic Five-in-a-row board, in which all kk-lines are either axis-parallel or diagonal. As long as the set of kk-lines considered here is totally determined by the ground set, we will simply use the ground set BB to represent the corresponding kk-board (B,ℒ)(B,\mathcal{L}).

Definition 2.2.

Let k,d∈ℕk,d\in\mathbb{N}. The set ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} along with the following kk-uniform subset family

{p+[0,k−1]d→:p∈ℤd,d→∈{−1,0,1}d\{0}}\displaystyle\left\{p+[0,k-1]\vec{d}\ :\ p\in\mathbb{Z}^{d},\ \vec{d}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0\}\right\}

is called the infinite kk-board of dimension dd. For ℓ=(ℓ1,ℓ2,⋯,ℓd)∈ℕd\ell=(\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\cdots,\ell_{d})\in\mathbb{N}^{d}, consider the hyper-rectangle B:=∏i=1d[ℓi]B:=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[\ell_{i}] and the family

ℒ:={p+[0,k−1]d→:p∈B,d→∈{−1,0,1}d\{0},p+[0,k−1]d→⊆B},\displaystyle\mathcal{L}:=\left\{p+[0,k-1]\vec{d}\ :\ p\in B,\ \vec{d}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0\},\ p+[0,k-1]\vec{d}\subseteq B\right\},

the board (B,ℒ)(B,\mathcal{L}) is called the (standard) kk-board of shape ℓ\ell. Further, consider the torus B′:=∏i=1d(ℤ/ℓi​ℤ)B^{\prime}:=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell_{i}\mathbb{Z}) and the family

ℒ′:={p+[0,k−1]d→:p∈B′,d→∈{−1,0,1}d\{0}},\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\prime}:=\left\{p+[0,k-1]\vec{d}\ :\ p\in B^{\prime},\ \vec{d}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0\}\right\},

we call (B′,ℒ′)(B^{\prime},\mathcal{L}^{\prime}) the toric kk-board of shape ℓ\ell.

Example 2.3.

The standard 55-board of shape (19,19)(19,19) corresponds to the board of the classical Five-in-a-row game.

Definition 2.4.

Given a kk-board (B,ℒ)(B,\mathcal{L}). A subset S⊆BS\subseteq B is called a configuration if it contains no near kk-line. The set of all configurations is denoted by 𝒞k​(B)\mathcal{C}_{k}(B). Further, a configuration SS is called saturated if it is maximal in 𝒞k​(B)\mathcal{C}_{k}(B) with respect to inclusion. We denote by 𝒮k​(B)\mathcal{S}_{k}(B) the family of all saturated configurations, i.e.,

𝒮k​(B):=max⁡({S⊆B:|L\S|≥2​∀L∈ℒ⁡(B)}).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{k}(B):=\max(\{S\subseteq B:|L\backslash S|\geq 2\ \forall L\in\mathcal{L}(B)\}).
Example 2.5.

On the board B=[k]dB=[k]^{d}, take k′:=k−2k^{\prime}:=k-2, one can find that every line LL with |B∩L|≥k′+1|B\cap L|\geq k^{\prime}+1 is either axis-parallel or diagonal. Thus the condition “No-(k′+1)(k^{\prime}+1)-in-line” agrees with near kk-line avoiding on this board.

One can verify that every saturated configuration corresponds to a game state right before the final two moves. Thus bounds on size of saturated configurations translate directly into bounds on the possible game lengths, up to an additive constant of 22. In the viewpoint of density, they are almost the same when the board size goes to infinity.

Definition 2.6.

Given a finite kk-board BB, the set

𝒟k​(B):={|S||B|:S∈𝒮k​(B)}\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{k}(B):=\left\{\frac{|S|}{|B|}:S\in\mathcal{S}_{k}(B)\right\}

is called the density spectrum of BB. We also define D⁡(k,B):=max⁡𝒟k​(B)D(k,B):=\max\mathcal{D}_{k}(B) and d⁡(k,B):=min⁡𝒟k​(B)d(k,B):=\min\mathcal{D}_{k}(B).

To define the extremal density for infinite grid board, we use the limit of that of finite grid boards.

Definition 2.7.

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, we define

D⁡(k,ℤ2):=limt→∞D⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)]) and d⁡(k,ℤ2):=limt→∞d⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)]),\displaystyle D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}):=\lim_{t\to\infty}D(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)])\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}):=\lim_{t\to\infty}d(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)]),

where m,n:ℕ→ℕm,n:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} are two arbitrary maps satisfying m⁡(t),n⁡(t)∈ω⁡(1)m(t),n(t)\in\omega(1).

The following two propositions provide the existence and well-definedness of these limits.

Proposition 2.8.

Given two maps m,n:ℕ→ℕm,n:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}. If m⁡(t),n⁡(t)∈ω⁡(1)m(t),n(t)\in\omega(1), then the limit of two sequences {D⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)])}t=1∞\{D(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)])\}_{t=1}^{\infty} and {d⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)])}t=1∞\{d(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)])\}_{t=1}^{\infty} exist.

Proposition 2.9.

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, there are two reals Lhigh,Llow∈(0,1)L_{\text{high}},L_{\text{low}}\in(0,1) such that

limt→∞D⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)])=Lhigh and limt→∞d⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)])=Llow\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}D(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)])=L_{\text{high}}\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ \lim_{t\to\infty}d(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)])=L_{\text{low}}

hold for every maps m,n:ℕ→ℕm,n:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} satisfying m⁡(t),n⁡(t)∈ω⁡(1)m(t),n(t)\in\omega(1).

The existence of the limit is based on the asymptotic monotonicity of those sequences. Roughly, we can build a bigger subset via tiling some small configurations, it produces configurations with density ε\varepsilon-close to that of building blocks. This method provides the monotonicity on far-tail terms of the sequence.

Lhigh:=lim supt→∞D⁡(t) and Llow:=lim inft→∞d⁡(t).\displaystyle L_{\text{high}}:=\limsup_{t\to\infty}D(t)\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ L_{\text{low}}:=\liminf_{t\to\infty}d(t).

Proof of Proposition 2.9.

Given two pairs (m0,n0)(m_{0},n_{0}) and (m1,n1)(m_{1},n_{1}) s.t. mi​(t),ni​(t)∈ω⁡(1)m_{i}(t),n_{i}(t)\in\omega(1) for i=0,1i=0,1. For i=0,1i=0,1, by Proposition 2.8, the limit of the sequence Si={D⁡(k,[mi​(t)]×[ni​(t)])}t=1∞S_{i}=\{D(k,[m_{i}(t)]\times[n_{i}(t)])\}_{t=1}^{\infty} exists, we call it LiL_{i}. Consider the mixed pair (m,n)(m,n) defined by

m⁡(t):=mr​(q) and n⁡(t):=nr​(q),m(t):=m_{r}(q)\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ n(t):=n_{r}(q),

where t=2​q+r∈ℕt=2q+r\in\mathbb{N}, q∈ℤ≥0q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\}. It is clear that m⁡(t),n⁡(t)∈ω⁡(1)m(t),n(t)\in\omega(1). By Proposition 2.8, the limit of S={D⁡(k,[m⁡(t)]×[n⁡(t)])}t=1∞S=\{D(k,[m(t)]\times[n(t)])\}_{t=1}^{\infty} exists, denoted by LhighL_{\text{high}}. As S0S_{0} and S1S_{1} are subsequences of SS, their limits agree with that of SS, i.e., L0=Lhigh=L1L_{0}=L_{\text{high}}=L_{1}. It suffices to prove the minimum density version by applying the same argument. ∎

In fact, these propositions could be generalized to higher dimension.

Proposition 2.10.

For k,n∈ℕk,n\in\mathbb{N}, D⁡(k,ℤn)D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and d⁡(k,ℤn)d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) exist and are well-defined.

3 Results for the Grid

In this section, we study the grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}. We obtain nearly tight bounds on D⁡(k,ℤ2)D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) (Theorem 1.2), establish upper and lower bounds on d⁡(k,ℤ2)d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) with gap 8​k−18k^{-1} (Theorem 1.3), and determine the exact values of D⁡(3,ℤ2)D(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) and d⁡(3,ℤ2)d(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) (Theorem 1.1).

Before proving these bounds, we show that the density spectrum of the grid forms an interval, so that it suffices to study the extremal densities.

Theorem 3.1.

For every k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} and α∈(d⁡(k,ℤ2),D⁡(k,ℤ2))ℝ\alpha\in(d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}),D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}))_{\mathbb{R}}, there is a sequence {Si}i=1∞\{S_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}, where Si∈𝒮k​([ℓi]2)S_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{k}([\ell_{i}]^{2}) for every i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, such that limi→∞|Si|ℓi2=α\lim\limits_{i\to\infty}\frac{|S_{i}|}{\ell_{i}^{2}}=\alpha.

M⟷S={(i,j)∈[ℓ]2:Mi,j=1}\displaystyle M\longleftrightarrow S=\{(i,j)\in[\ell]^{2}:M_{i,j}=1\}

and define the density δ⁡(M):=1ℓ2​|{(i,j):Mi,j=1}|\delta(M):=\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}|\{(i,j):M_{i,j}=1\}|. Let M¯\overline{M} denote the matrix obtained from MM by adding a layer of zeros around it, i.e.,

M¯:=(0000000M1,1M1,2⋯M1,ℓ00M2,1M2,2⋯M2,ℓ00⋱00Mℓ,1Mℓ,2⋯Mℓ,ℓ0000000)∈Mℓ+2​({0,1}).\displaystyle\overline{M}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0&0&0\\ 0&M_{1,1}&M_{1,2}&\cdots&M_{1,\ell}&0\\ 0&M_{2,1}&M_{2,2}&\cdots&M_{2,\ell}&0\\ 0&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&0\\ 0&M_{\ell,1}&M_{\ell,2}&\cdots&M_{\ell,\ell}&0\\ 0&0&0&0&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}\in M_{\ell+2}(\{0,1\}).

3.1 Nearly Tight Bounds on D⁡(k,ℤ2)D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})

We split the proof into two parts: the upper bound and the lower bound. For the upper bound, we introduce the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

For k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}, let BB be a finite kk-board and ℒ⋆\mathcal{L}^{\star} be a family of pairwise-disjoint kk-lines. Then D⁡(k,B)≤1−2k+2​|R|k​|B|D(k,B)\leq 1-\frac{2}{k}+\frac{2|R|}{k|B|}, where R=R(ℒ⋆):=B\(∪L∈ℒ⋆L)R=R(\mathcal{L}^{\star}):=B\backslash(\cup_{L\in\mathcal{L}^{\star}}L).

By this lemma, for every ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, as the disjoint horizontal kk-lines family

ℒℓ:={(x,y)+[0,k−1](1,0):x∈1+k[0,ℓ−1],y∈[kℓ]}\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\ell}:=\{(x,y)+[0,k-1](1,0):x\in 1+k[0,\ell-1],\ y\in[k\ell]\}

forms a partition of [k​ℓ]2[k\ell]^{2}, we have

D⁡(k,[k​ℓ]2)≤1−2k+2​|R|k​|B|=1−2k\displaystyle D(k,[k\ell]^{2})\leq 1-\frac{2}{k}+\frac{2|R|}{k|B|}=1-\frac{2}{k}

since R⁡(ℒℓ)=∅R(\mathcal{L}_{\ell})=\emptyset. Consequently, we obtain the upper bound

D⁡(k,ℤ2)=limℓ→∞D⁡(k,[k​ℓ]2)≤1−2k.\displaystyle D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=\lim_{\ell\to\infty}D(k,[k\ell]^{2})\leq 1-\frac{2}{k}.
Proof of Lemma 3.2.

Let S∈𝒮k​(B)S\in\mathcal{S}_{k}(B) be a saturated configuration reaching maximum density. By the definition of configuration, we have |S∩L|≤k−2|S\cap L|\leq k-2 for every kk-line LL, which implies

|S|=∑L∈ℒ⋆|S∩L|+|S∩R|≤(k−2)​|ℒ⋆|+|R|=(1−2k)​|B|+2k​|R|.\displaystyle|S|=\sum_{L\in\mathcal{L}^{\star}}|S\cap L|+|S\cap R|\leq(k-2)|\mathcal{L}^{\star}|+|R|=\left(1-\frac{2}{k}\right)|B|+\frac{2}{k}|R|.

Dividing both sides by |B||B|, we get

D⁡(k,B)=|S||B|≤1−2k+2​|R|k​|B|.\displaystyle D(k,B)=\frac{|S|}{|B|}\leq 1-\frac{2}{k}+\frac{2|R|}{k|B|}.

∎

The lower bound is based on Lemma 3.3, which provides required lower bound when kk is not a multiple of 33.

Lemma 3.3.

For k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} with 3∤k3\nmid k, we have D⁡(k,ℤ2)≥1−2k.D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\geq 1-\frac{2}{k}.

For the case that kk is a multiple of 33, noting that, in a hyper-rectangle, every near kk-line contains a near (k−1)(k-1)-line, hence near (k−1)(k-1)-line avoidance implies near kk-line avoidance. In particular, we have 𝒞k−1​([ℓ]2)⊆𝒞k​([ℓ]2)\mathcal{C}_{k-1}([\ell]^{2})\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{k}([\ell]^{2}), which implies

D⁡(k,[ℓ]2)≥D⁡(k−1,[ℓ]2).\displaystyle D(k,[\ell]^{2})\geq D(k-1,[\ell]^{2}).

Combining Lemma 3.3, we derive D⁡(k,ℤ2)≥D⁡(k−1,ℤ2)≥1−2k−1D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\geq D(k-1,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\geq 1-\frac{2}{k-1}.

To prove this lemma, we construct a configuration by removing zero set of some equations. Being an algebraic structure, a zero set is expected to have nearly the same number of points in any given line segments.

Proof of Lemma 3.3.

Given k∈ℕ≥2k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} with 3∤k3\nmid k, we define

Z⁡(r):={x=(x1,x2)∈ℤ2:x1+2​x2=r(modk)}\displaystyle Z(r):=\{\ x=(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\ :\ x_{1}+2x_{2}=r\pmod{k}\}

for each r∈[0,k−1]r\in[0,k-1]. First, we claim that the equality |L∩Z⁡(0)|+|L∩Z⁡(1)|=2|L\cap Z(0)|+|L\cap Z(1)|=2 holds for every kk-line on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}. Fix a such kk-line L=v+[0,k−1]​d→L=v+[0,k-1]\vec{d}, where v∈ℤ2v\in\mathbb{Z}^{2} and d→∈{−1,0,1}2\{0}\vec{d}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{2}\backslash\{0\}. Note that v+a​d→∈Z⁡(r)v+a\vec{d}\in Z(r) if and only if

(d1+2​d2)​a=r−(v1+2​v2)(modk).\displaystyle(d_{1}+2d_{2})a=r-(v_{1}+2v_{2})\pmod{k}.

If d1+2​d2d_{1}+2d_{2} and kk are coprime, there is a unique solution in [0,k−1][0,k-1] to the equation. In this case, we have

|L∩Z⁡(0)|+|L∩Z⁡(1)|=1+1=2.\displaystyle|L\cap Z(0)|+|L\cap Z(1)|=1+1=2.

As all possible values of d1+2​d2d_{1}+2d_{2} are ±1\pm 1, ±2\pm 2, and ±3\pm 3, the only non-coprime case is d1+2​d2=±2d_{1}+2d_{2}=\pm 2 and k∈2​ℕk\in 2\mathbb{N}. In this case, the equation has zero or two solutions depending on the parity of r−(v1+2​v2)r-(v_{1}+2v_{2}). Since 0−(v1+2​v2)0-(v_{1}+2v_{2}) and 1−(v1+2​v2)1-(v_{1}+2v_{2}) must have different parity, it leads to |L∩Z⁡(0)|+|L∩Z⁡(1)|=2|L\cap Z(0)|+|L\cap Z(1)|=2. Consider the subset Sℓ:=[ℓ]2\(Z⁡(0)⊔Z⁡(1))S_{\ell}:=[\ell]^{2}\backslash(Z(0)\sqcup Z(1)) in the board [ℓ]2[\ell]^{2}. By the claim, it is near kk-line avoiding since it misses exactly two points from every kk-line. Therefore, Sℓ∈𝒞k​([ℓ]2)S_{\ell}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}([\ell]^{2}). For every ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, the family ℒℓ\mathcal{L}_{\ell} defined above is a partition of [k​ℓ]2[k\ell]^{2} consisting of kk-lines. Hence

|Sk​ℓ|=∑L∈ℒℓ|Sk​ℓ∩L|=∑L∈ℒℓ(k−2)=|ℒℓ|​(k−2)=(k​ℓ)2​(1−2k).\displaystyle|S_{k\ell}|=\sum_{L\in\mathcal{L}_{\ell}}|S_{k\ell}\cap L|=\sum_{L\in\mathcal{L}_{\ell}}(k-2)=|\mathcal{L}_{\ell}|(k-2)=(k\ell)^{2}\left(1-\frac{2}{k}\right).

Then we obtain D⁡(k,ℤ2)=limℓ→∞D⁡(k,[k​ℓ]2)≥limℓ→∞|Sk​ℓ|(k​ℓ)2=1−2k.D(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=\lim\limits_{\ell\to\infty}D(k,[k\ell]^{2})\geq\lim\limits_{\ell\to\infty}\frac{|S_{k\ell}|}{(k\ell)^{2}}=1-\frac{2}{k}. ∎

3.2 Bounds on d⁡(k,ℤ2)d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})

To lower bound d⁡(k,ℤ2)d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2}), given a saturated configuration S∈𝒮k​([ℓ]2)S\in\mathcal{S}_{k}([\ell]^{2}), we count the number of pairs of points inside and outside of SS lying in some kk-line. Then we obtain a relation between |S||S| and |[ℓ]2\S||[\ell]^{2}\backslash S|; in particular, it implies:

Lemma 3.4.

For k,ℓ∈ℕ≥2k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}, we have d⁡(k,[ℓ]2)≥k−216+(k−2)=1−16​k−1−o⁡(k−1).d(k,[\ell]^{2})\geq\frac{k-2}{16+(k-2)}=1-16k^{-1}-o(k^{-1}).

Proof of Lemma 3.4.

The bound is trivial for k=2k=2, hence we assume k≥3k\geq 3. Let S∈𝒮k​([ℓ]2)S\in\mathcal{S}_{k}([\ell]^{2}) be a saturated configuration reaching minimum density. Define N:=[ℓ]2\SN:=[\ell]^{2}\backslash S. Consider the bipartite graph G=(N⊔S,E)G=(N\sqcup S,E) defined by

E:={{x,y}:x∈N,y∈S,∃ near k-line L s.t. y∈L⊆S∪{x}}.\displaystyle E:=\big\{\{x,y\}:x\in N,\ y\in S,\ \exists\text{ near $k$-line $L$ s.t. }y\in L\subseteq S\cup\{x\}\big\}.

Given a x∈Nx\in N, as S∪{x}∉𝒞k​([ℓ]2)S\cup\{x\}\not\in\mathcal{C}_{k}([\ell]^{2}), there is a near kk-line L⊆S∪{x}L\subseteq S\cup\{x\}. By the definition of GG, we have L\{x}⊆NG​(x)L\backslash\{x\}\subseteq N_{G}(x), hence δ⁡(N)≥k−2\delta(N)\geq k-2. Conversely, given a y∈Sy\in S and a direction d→∈{−1,0,1}2\{0}\vec{d}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{2}\backslash\{0\}. For every i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, let ni∈ℕn_{i}\in\mathbb{N} be the integer such that xi:=y+ni​d→x_{i}:=y+n_{i}\vec{d} is the ii-th empty position in the direction d→\vec{d} starting from yy. Note that, for any kk-line LL containing both yy and xix_{i}, there are i−1i-1 points in LL, say x1,x2,⋯,xi−1x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{i-1}, not included in S∪{xi}S\cup\{x_{i}\}. Therefore, xi∉NG​(y)x_{i}\not\in N_{G}(y) if i≥3i\geq 3. As there are eight directions, we have Δ⁡(S)≤8×2=16\Delta(S)\leq 8\times 2=16. Count the number of edges in GG, we get

(k−2)​|N|=δ⁡(N)​|N|≤|E⁡(G)|≤Δ⁡(S)|S|≤16​|S|,\displaystyle(k-2)|N|=\delta(N)|N|\leq|E(G)|\leq\Delta(S)|S|\leq 16|S|,

which means |N|≤16k−2​|S||N|\leq\frac{16}{k-2}|S|. Then the minimum density is bounded below by

d⁡(k,[ℓ]2)=|S|ℓ2=|S||N|+|S|≥|S|16k−2​|S|+|S|=k−216+(k−2).d(k,[\ell]^{2})=\frac{|S|}{\ell^{2}}=\frac{|S|}{|N|+|S|}\geq\frac{|S|}{\frac{16}{k-2}|S|+|S|}=\frac{k-2}{16+(k-2)}.

∎

The upper bound is obtained via a specific construction. The key idea is that minimizing the number of points needed to control a given region yields a stronger upper bound. In particular, a filled (k−2)×(k−2)(k-2)\times(k-2) square almost controls the surrounding (k+2)×(k+2)(k+2)\times(k+2) square, in which each point controls at least four kk-lines, making it a natural candidate for the construction. By tiling such pattern, we get:

Lemma 3.5.

For k∈ℕ≥4k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 4}, we have d⁡(k,ℤ2)≤(k−2)2+8(k+2)2=1−8​k−1+o⁡(k−1).d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\leq\frac{(k-2)^{2}+8}{(k+2)^{2}}=1-8k^{-1}+o(k^{-1}).

Proof of Lemma 3.5.

Consider the following subset inside [k+2]2[k+2]^{2}: The square [3,k]2[3,k]^{2} in the center along with eight points surrounding each corners of the ground set

{(1,2),(2,1),(k+1,1),(k+2,2),(k+2,k+1),(k+1,k+2),(2,k+2),(1,k+1)}.\{(1,2),(2,1),(k+1,1),(k+2,2),(k+2,k+1),(k+1,k+2),(2,k+2),(1,k+1)\}.

We call this subset ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}, check the figure 1 for the example k=5k=5.

Note that, when k≥4k\geq 4, such pattern contains no near kk-line and adding any remaining point in the ground set [k+2]2[k+2]^{2} creates a near kk-line within the ground set. For ℓ=n⁡(k+2)∈(k+2)​ℕ\ell=n(k+2)\in(k+2)\mathbb{N}, let SS be the subset built by tiling ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} over [ℓ]2[\ell]^{2}. In particular, we define

S:=⋃v∈((k+2)​[0,n−1])2ℱk+v.\displaystyle S:=\bigcup_{v\in((k+2)[0,n-1])^{2}}\mathcal{F}_{k}+v.

It is clear that SS contains no near kk-lines. Given a point x∈[ℓ]2\Sx\in[\ell]^{2}\backslash S, let vx∈((k+2)​[0,n−1])2v_{x}\in((k+2)[0,n-1])^{2} be such that x∈[k+2]2+vxx\in[k+2]^{2}+v_{x}. By the property of ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}, we know there is a near kk-line in ℱk∪{x−vx}\mathcal{F}_{k}\cup\{x-v_{x}\}. In other words, S∪{x}⊇(ℱk∪{x−vx})+vxS\cup\{x\}\supseteq(\mathcal{F}_{k}\cup\{x-v_{x}\})+v_{x} has a near kk-line particularly inside [k+2]2+vx[k+2]^{2}+v_{x}. Therefore, as SS is saturated, we have the upper bound

d⁡(k,[ℓ]2)≤|S|ℓ2=ℓ2(k+2)2​|ℱk|ℓ2=(k−2)2+8(k+2)2.\displaystyle d(k,[\ell]^{2})\leq\frac{|S|}{\ell^{2}}=\frac{\frac{\ell^{2}}{(k+2)^{2}}|\mathcal{F}_{k}|}{\ell^{2}}=\frac{(k-2)^{2}+8}{(k+2)^{2}}.

∎

Note that eight points around corners in ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} dominate when kk is small. In addition, these points control no points at all.33 3 Although, they do control some points when k=4k=4, but those points are also controlled by the central square from other tiles. Therefore, they are still redundant when minimizing the density. A better bound for k≤8k\leq 8 could be obtained by removing these points. Consider ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} but removing these points from the ground set, denoted by ℱk′\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\prime}.

Consider the covering shown in Figure 3.

Let S′S^{\prime} be the union of ℱk′\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\prime} in the covering and CC be the union of ground sets. It is clear that S′S^{\prime} is near kk-line avoiding. Let S′′∈𝒮k​([ℓ]2)S^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{k}([\ell]^{2}) be the saturated configuration containing S′S^{\prime}. As S′S^{\prime} is already saturated inside CC, we know

|S′′∩C||C|=|S′∩C||C|=(k−2)2k2+2​k+2.\displaystyle\frac{|S^{\prime\prime}\cap C|}{|C|}=\frac{|S^{\prime}\cap C|}{|C|}=\frac{(k-2)^{2}}{k^{2}+2k+2}.

Further, the difference S′′\CS^{\prime\prime}\backslash C lies in the band of width k+1k+1 from the border, i.e., |S′\S|≤4​(k+1)​ℓ|S^{\prime}\backslash S|\leq 4(k+1)\ell. Then we may conclude that

d⁡(k,[ℓ]2)≤|S′′|ℓ2=|S′′∩C|ℓ2+|S′′\C|ℓ2≤(k−2)2k2+2​k+2+4​(k+1)ℓ,\displaystyle d(k,[\ell]^{2})\leq\frac{|S^{\prime\prime}|}{\ell^{2}}=\frac{|S^{\prime\prime}\cap C|}{\ell^{2}}+\frac{|S^{\prime\prime}\backslash C|}{\ell^{2}}\leq\frac{(k-2)^{2}}{k^{2}+2k+2}+\frac{4(k+1)}{\ell},

which leads to the following lemma.

Lemma 3.6.

For k∈ℕ≥3k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}, we have d⁡(k,ℤ2)≤(k−2)2k2+2​k+2=1−6​k−1+o⁡(k−1).d(k,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\leq\frac{(k-2)^{2}}{k^{2}+2k+2}=1-6k^{-1}+o(k^{-1}).

Notably, this construction works for the case k=3k=3 but has a loose bound than Lemma 3.5 as kk grows.

3.3 Determining D⁡(3,ℤ2)D(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) and d⁡(3,ℤ2)d(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2})

For k=3k=3, according to Lemma 3.4 and Lemma 3.6, we have

117=3−216+(3−2)≤d⁡(3,ℤ2)≤(3−2)232+6+2=117,\displaystyle\frac{1}{17}=\frac{3-2}{16+(3-2)}\leq d(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\leq\frac{(3-2)^{2}}{3^{2}+6+2}=\frac{1}{17},

i.e., the minimum density is known. For the maximum density, we first lower bound it by a specific configuration, then we show that any saturated configuration reaching maximum density must be isomorphic to such configuration.

Theorem 3.7.

D⁡(3,ℤ2)=15D(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2})=\frac{1}{5}.

Proof of Theorem 3.7.

Consider the subset

Z:={x→∈ℤ2:⟨(2,−1),x→⟩=1(mod5)}.\displaystyle Z:=\{\vec{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\ :\ \langle(2,-1),\vec{x}\rangle=1\pmod{5}\}.

For each ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, we define Sℓ:=[ℓ]2∩ZS_{\ell}:=[\ell]^{2}\cap Z. See Figure 5 for an illustration of S10S_{10}. Note that

⟨(2,−1),{−1,0,1}2\{0}⟩={±1,±2,±3}\langle(2,-1),\{-1,0,1\}^{2}\backslash\{0\}\rangle=\{\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3\}

For ℓ∈5​ℕ\ell\in 5\mathbb{N}, [ℓ]2[\ell]^{2} can be partitioned into horizontal 55-lines. Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be a such partition, then we can lower bound the maximum density by

Let ℓ\ell go to infinity, we derive D⁡(3,ℤ2)≥15D(3,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\geq\frac{1}{5}.

We now upper bound the maximum density. Given a saturated configuration S∈𝒮3​([ℓ]2)S\in\mathcal{S}_{3}([\ell]^{2}). For every x∈[2,ℓ−1]2∩Sx\in[2,\ell-1]^{2}\cap S, its four adjacent points, x+(±1,0)x+(\pm 1,0) and x+(0,±1)x+(0,\pm 1), are not in SS; otherwise, SS would not be near 33-line avoiding. Such case happens only if

By the discussion above, we have

|E⁡(G)|=∑x∈SdG​(x)≥∑x∈S∩[2,ℓ−1]24=4​|S∩[2,ℓ−1]2|≥4​(|S|−4​ℓ).\displaystyle|E(G)|=\sum_{x\in S}d_{G}(x)\geq\sum_{x\in S\cap[2,\ell-1]^{2}}4=4|S\cap[2,\ell-1]^{2}|\geq 4(|S|-4\ell).

for sufficient large ℓ\ell. Hence, there is v=v⁡(ℓ)v=v(\ell) such that

|Sℓ,v|k⁡(2​k−1)≤1−2k.\frac{|S_{\ell,v}|}{k(2k-1)}\leq 1-\frac{2}{k}.

4 Results for Hypercubes

In this section, we study hypercubes [k]d[k]^{d} for d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. We obtain bounds on D⁡(k,[k]d)D(k,[k]^{d}) with gap C​k−2Ck^{-2}, where CC is a constant depending only on dd (Theorem 1.4), and derive exact values of d⁡(k,[k]d)d(k,[k]^{d}) (Theorem 1.5).

4.1 Bounds on D⁡(k,[k]d)D(k,[k]^{d})

The upper bound is simple. As [k]d[k]^{d} can be partitioned into a number of kk-lines, by Lemma 3.2, we have D⁡(k,[k]d)≤1−2kD(k,[k]^{d})\leq 1-\frac{2}{k}. The lower bound follows the spirit of proof of Lemma 3.3. However, instead of removing two zero sets from the board, we first partition the board into hypercubes, then remove a zero set from each part.

Lemma 4.1.

For every d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, there are constants C=C⁡(d)>0C=C(d)>0 and N=N⁡(d)∈ℕN=N(d)\in\mathbb{N} such that

D⁡(k,[k]d)≥1−2k−Ck2\displaystyle D(k,[k]^{d})\geq 1-\frac{2}{k}-\frac{C}{k^{2}}

holds for k≥Nk\geq N.

Proof of Lemma 4.1.

Let ℓ=ℓ⁡(k,d)\ell=\ell(k,d) be the largest integer not greater than k2\frac{k}{2} such that it is coprime with ii for every i∈[d]i\in[d]. Clearly, the difference btween k2\frac{k}{2} and ℓ\ell is not greater than d!d!. Like the proof of Lemma 3.3, for every r∈ℤr\in\mathbb{Z}, we define

Z⁡(r):={x→∈ℤd:⟨(1,1,⋯,1),x→⟩=r(modℓ)}.\displaystyle Z(r):=\{\ \vec{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}\ :\ \langle(1,1,\cdots,1),\vec{x}\rangle=r\pmod{\ell}\}.

We claim that, for every ℓ\ell-line L=x+[0,ℓ−1]​d→L=x+[0,\ell-1]\vec{d} on ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} with d→∈{0,1}d\{0}\vec{d}\in\{0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0\}, we have |L∩Z⁡(1)|=1|L\cap Z(1)|=1. Recall that, as in the proof of Lemma 3.3, we have

|L∩Z⁡(r)|=1 if and only ifgcd⁡(⟨(1,1,⋯,1),d→⟩,ℓ)=1.\displaystyle|L\cap Z(r)|=1\ \ \text{ if and only if}\ \ \gcd(\langle(1,1,\cdots,1),\vec{d}\rangle,\ell)=1.

Note that, for d→∈{0,1}t\{0}\vec{d}\in\{0,1\}^{t}\backslash\{0\}, we have ⟨(1,1,⋯,1),d→⟩=∥d→∥1∈[d]\langle(1,1,\cdots,1),\vec{d}\rangle=\lVert\vec{d}\rVert_{1}\in[d]. Then, as ℓ\ell is coprime with [d][d], the claim is proved. Set B=B⁡(ℓ,d):=[0,ℓ−1]d\Z⁡(1)B=B(\ell,d):=[0,\ell-1]^{d}\backslash Z(1). In the following, we will use projections and reflections of BB as the building blocks to form a configuration S⋆=S⋆​(k,d)∈𝒞k​([k]d)S^{\star}=S^{\star}(k,d)\in\mathcal{C}_{k}([k]^{d}) such that

|S⋆|kd≥1−2k−4​d!(k−2​d!)​k.\displaystyle\frac{|S^{\star}|}{k^{d}}\geq 1-\frac{2}{k}-\frac{4d!}{(k-2d!)k}.

With such configuration, let C⁡(d):=8​d!C(d):=8d! and N⁡(d):=4​d!N(d):=4d!, then we derive

D⁡(k,[k]d)≥|S⋆|kd≥1−2k−4​d!(k−2​d!)​k≥1−2k−Ck2\displaystyle D(k,[k]^{d})\geq\frac{|S^{\star}|}{k^{d}}\geq 1-\frac{2}{k}-\frac{4d!}{(k-2d!)k}\geq 1-\frac{2}{k}-\frac{C}{k^{2}}

for k≥Nk\geq N, closing the proof. ∎

Building up the configuration S⋆S^{\star}

We start with defining the core X:=[ℓ,k−ℓ+1]dX:=[\ell,k-\ell+1]^{d}, a hypercube centered in [k]d[k]^{d}. Also, we define its interior int​X:=[ℓ+1,k−ℓ]d\text{int}X:=[\ell+1,k-\ell]^{d} and boundary ∂X:=X\int​X\partial X:=X\backslash\text{int}X. For each point xx in the core, we paste a modified building block ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) on it. The map ϕ\phi is defined by

ϕ:X\displaystyle\phi:X →{2ℤd→2ℤd}\displaystyle\to\left\{2^{\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\to 2^{\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\right\}
x\displaystyle x ↦[Y↦Rrev​(x)(Y)∩Eint​(x)],\displaystyle\mapsto\left[Y\mapsto R_{\text{rev}(x)}(Y)\cap E_{\text{int}(x)}\right],

where rev​(x):=x−1​(ℓ)⊆[d]\text{rev}(x):=x^{-1}(\ell)\subseteq[d] and int​(x):=x−1​([ℓ+1,k−ℓ])⊆[d]\text{int}(x):=x^{-1}([\ell+1,k-\ell])\subseteq[d] are the set of reversing and interior indices respectively; RIR_{I} negates the ii-th coordinate for each i∈Ii\in I, and EJE_{J} is the subspace of ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} with the jj-th coordinate zero for each j∈Jj\in J. Define

S⋆:=⨆x∈X(x+ϕ⁡(x)​(B))⊆[k]d.\displaystyle S^{\star}:=\bigsqcup\limits_{x\in X}(x+\phi(x)(B))\subseteq[k]^{d}.

Figure 6 displays S⋆S^{\star} and several types of building blocks for k=8k=8 and d=2d=2.

In this example, for xx, we paste the original BB on it; for yy, the block but negating the 22-th coordinate is pasted; for zz and ww, in order to fit in the space [k]d[k]^{d}, the blocks are truncated on E2E_{2} and E{1,2}E_{\{1,2\}}, respectively.

Before we verify that S⋆S^{\star} is a configuration, we first lower bound the density of this subset. Given x∈Xx\in X, if x∈int​Xx\in\text{int}X, ϕ​(x)​(B)\phi(x)(B) is a single point and |int​(x)|=d|\text{int}(x)|=d. If x∈∂Xx\in\partial X, the ground space ϕ⁡(x)​([0,ℓ−1]d)\phi(x)([0,\ell-1]^{d}) can be partitioned into ℓd−1−|int​(x)|\ell^{d-1-|\text{int}(x)|} ℓ\ell-lines of direction in {0,1}d\{0}\{0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0\}. By the claim above, we know |L∩ϕ⁡(x)​(B)|=ℓ−1|L\cap\phi(x)(B)|=\ell-1 for every LL in the partition, hence we obtain |ϕ⁡(x)​(B)|=(ℓ−1)​ℓd−1−|int​(x)||\phi(x)(B)|=(\ell-1)\ell^{d-1-|\text{int}(x)|}. In either case, we have

(2) d⁡(x):=|ϕ​(x)​(B)||ϕ⁡(x)​([0,ℓ−1]d)|≥(ℓ−1)​ℓd−1−|int​(x)|ℓd−|int​(x)|=1−1ℓ.\displaystyle d(x):=\frac{|\phi(x)(B)|}{|\phi(x)([0,\ell-1]^{d})|}\geq\frac{(\ell-1)\ell^{d-1-|\text{int}(x)|}}{\ell^{d-|\text{int}(x)|}}=1-\frac{1}{\ell}.

As the ground spaces {ϕ⁡(x)​([0,ℓ−1]d)}x∈X\{\phi(x)([0,\ell-1]^{d})\}_{x\in X} form a partition of [k]d[k]^{d}, |S⋆|kd\frac{|S^{\star}|}{k^{d}} can be regarded as the weighted-average of {d⁡(x)}x∈X\{d(x)\}_{x\in X} by setting the weight of xx to be |ϕ⁡(x)​([0,ℓ−1]d)||\phi(x)([0,\ell-1]^{d})|. Then (2) implies that |S⋆|kd≥1−1ℓ\frac{|S^{\star}|}{k^{d}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{\ell}. Hence, by ℓ>k2−d!\ell>\frac{k}{2}-d!, we obtain the desired lower bound

|S⋆|kd≥1−1ℓ=1−2​ℓℓ​k−k−2​ℓℓ​k≥1−2k−4​d!(k−2​d!)​k.\displaystyle\frac{|S^{\star}|}{k^{d}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{\ell}=1-\frac{2\ell}{\ell k}-\frac{k-2\ell}{\ell k}\geq 1-\frac{2}{k}-\frac{4d!}{(k-2d!)k}.

Near kk-line Avoidance

Claim 4.2.

For every kk-line LL in [k]d[k]^{d}, there are two points x,y∈Xx,y\in X such that

|x+ϕ⁡(x)​([0,ℓ−1]d)∩L|=|y+ϕ⁡(y)​([0,ℓ−1]d)∩L|=ℓ.|x+\phi(x)([0,\ell-1]^{d})\cap L|=|y+\phi(y)([0,\ell-1]^{d})\cap L|=\ell.

In particular, Rrev​(x)−1​(L−x)R_{\text{rev}(x)}^{-1}(L-x) and Rrev​(y)−1​(L−y)R_{\text{rev}(y)}^{-1}(L-y) are ℓ\ell-lines with direction in {0,1}d\{0}\{0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0\}.

With this claim, it is sufficient to show the near kk-line forbiddenness of S⋆S^{\star}. Given a kk-line LL, let x,yx,y be such points in Claim 4.2. Following the previous claim, we can see that S⋆S^{\star} misses two points on LL, one from x+ϕ⁡(x)​([0,ℓ−1]d\B)x+\phi(x)([0,\ell-1]^{d}\backslash B) and the other from y+ϕ⁡(y)​([0,ℓ−1]d\B)y+\phi(y)([0,\ell-1]^{d}\backslash B). As a consequence, S⋆S^{\star} contains no near kk-lines, i.e., S⋆∈𝒞k​([k]d)S^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}([k]^{d}).

5.2 Extensions

Winner Determination

For a fixed board BB, the monochromatic kk-in-a-row game is a finite perfect-information game, and hence the outcome is determined: it is either a first-player win (FP), a second-player win (SP), or a draw. In this setting, draws occur if and only if the family of kk-lines is empty, which is a degenerate case that we typically exclude, so the game is either FP or SP.

Unlike many positional games, the strategy-stealing argument does not apply here, as the additional move available to the first player may be disadvantageous; in particular, the first player cannot always guarantee a win. A natural problem is to determine the winning player for a given board BB, or more ambitiously, to describe an explicit winning strategy.

For instance, the outcome on [k]d[k]^{d} is completely characterized: it is FP when kk is odd and SP when kk is even. This result comes from a pairing strategy for the winning player. See pages 46-48 in [8] for the construction.

Biased Game

One natural extension is the biased (p:q)(p:q) game, in which the first and second players claim pp and qq points per move, respectively. The cases p≥kp\geq k or q≥kq\geq k are trivial, so we restrict to max⁡{p,q}<k\max\{p,q\}<k.

A heuristic suggests that the player with the larger bias should have an advantage, and this is indeed the case when the board is sufficiently large. Let Alice and Bob denote the players with biases α\alpha and β\beta, respectively, and suppose α>β\alpha>\beta. Consider the quantity NN, defined as the minimum number of points needed to complete a kk-line from the current state. Alice’s strategy is based on the value of NN: If N≤αN\leq\alpha, Alice wins without doubt. If not, Alice claims α\alpha points such that NN is decreased by 11. (This can be done once the board size is large enough.) In this setting, Bob cannot win; otherwise, one would obtain a contradiction β≥N−1≥α\beta\geq N-1\geq\alpha before the very last move. Consequently, the most interesting case is the balanced biased (p:p)(p:p) game with 1<p<k1<p<k, where the advantage of larger bias disappears.

Multiplayer Games

For t∈ℕ≥3t\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}, we can consider the tt-player variant: There are tt players. Each player, in turns, claims a position from the board until a kk-line is created. It comes a natural question: Under this circumstance, which player will win the game? Although it is similar to the 22-player game, but there are some cases that, at some moment, a player cannot win but their move can determine the winner. For instance, consider the 55-player monochromatic 33-in a row played on [3]2[3]^{2}: If player 11 starts with taking (2,2)(2,2), then player 33 wins. If player 11 starts with taking other point, only player 33, 44, and 55 have chance to win. In either case, player 11 cannot win.


Thus, further analysis requires additional restrictions or assumptions on the players.

ss-Saturated Configurations

We can extract the concept of saturated configuration and quantize it. Given a kk-board BB. For every s∈[k]s\in[k], we define the ss-configurations

𝒞k,s​(B):={S⊆B:|L\S|≥s​∀ k-line L}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{k,s}(B):=\{S\subseteq B:|L\backslash S|\geq s\ \forall\text{ $k$-line $L$}\}.

Then we accordingly define the saturated ss-configurations, 𝒮k,s​(B)\mathcal{S}_{k,s}(B). Further, if BB is finite, we also define ss-density spectrum, 𝒟k,s​(B)\mathcal{D}_{k,s}(B), and extremal ss-densities, Ds​(k,B)D_{s}(k,B) and ds​(k,B)d_{s}(k,B). Notably, the original problem is corresponding to the case s=2s=2.

Several results can be extended to this setting. For instance, by the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 3.2, we can obtain

Ds​(k,B)≤1−sk+s​|R|k​|B|\displaystyle D_{s}(k,B)\leq 1-\frac{s}{k}+\frac{s|R|}{k|B|}

for every s∈[k]s\in[k], where RR is the complement of union of some disjoint kk-lines. And, by adapting the proof of Lemma 3.4, we have

ds​(k,B)≥k−ss​N​(B)+(k−s),\displaystyle d_{s}(k,B)\geq\frac{k-s}{sN(B)+(k-s)},

where N⁡(B):=maxx∈B⁡|{k-lines containing x}|N(B):=\max_{x\in B}|\{\text{$k$-lines containing $x$}\}|. See pages 54-58 in [8] for detailed proofs. However, bounds obtained from specific constructions still require further discussion and modification.

Extremal Board Problem

The original monochromatic kk in a row problem asks how large or small the density of a saturated configuration on a given board can be.A related question is the following: for a fixed board size nn, which boards maximize or minimize the extremal densities? To formalize this question, we restrict attention to nn-subsets of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}. For every B∈(ℤ2n)B\in\binom{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}{n}, we regard BB as a board by defining

ℒ(B):={L:L is a k-line on ℤ2,L⊆B}.\mathcal{L}(B):=\{L:L\text{ is a $k$-line on $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$},\ L\subseteq B\}.

Then the question is to determine the terms

Dmin​(k,n):=minB∈(ℤ2n)⁡D⁡(k,B) and dmax​(k,n):=maxB∈(ℤ2n)⁡d⁡(k,B).\displaystyle D_{\min}(k,n):=\min_{B\in\binom{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}{n}}D(k,B)\ \ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ \ d_{\max}(k,n):=\max_{B\in\binom{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}{n}}d(k,B).

However, without additional assumptions determining dmax​(k,n)d_{\max}(k,n) becomes trivial. Indeed, if a point x∈Bx\in B is not contained in any kk-line of BB, then xx must belong to every saturated configuration. In fact, for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we can find a nn-subset containing no kk-line, it implies dmax​(k,n)=1d_{\max}(k,n)=1. Therefore, it is natural to consider subsets that every point is contained in some kk-lines.
